title: Fisher Glasses: Tail-Certified Quantum Metrology in Quenched Environments
abstract: Quantum metrological advantage is certified by averaged Fisher responses: contrast, susceptibility, or quantum Fisher information (QFI). This fails in quenched sensors, where slow environmental variables freeze within a session but vary between repetitions: shallow nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, superconducting qubits with slow two-level fluctuators, and semiconductor spin qubits in drifting charge noise. They sample session-resolved Fisher geometries, not an averaged channel. Certification conditions on the latent session, projects nuisance directions, inverts to attainable loss, then tail-certifies; this inverse upper-tail loss defines quenched tail-certified information. A no-go theorem: no averaged Fisher data determine this certificate; ensembles sharing averaged Fisher matrix, QFI, and projected information have finite or zero certified precision. A Fisher-zero integrability transition governs collapse: the inverse-loss tail exponent $β$ sets the boundary, with nonintegrable certified loss for $β\le 1$, even when annealed information is large or scaling. The certified quantum resource is response transverse to latent disorder, not raw amplification sharing its generator; universal design laws: safe windows, nondegenerate portfolios, Fisher reserves, action separation, Fisher-cut criteria. A shallow-NV Ramsey tournament shows average-QFI optimization is tail-catastrophic, whereas tail-certified designs recover nearly three orders of magnitude in certified information at equal shot budget and latent ensemble. These non-self-averaging phases are Fisher glasses, governed by Fisher-zero rare-event statistics.
summary: The paper addresses the failure of standard quantum metrology bounds when environmental noise is 'quenched' rather than averaged over. It introduces Tail-Certified Information ($	ext{ITC}_\alpha$) using Conditional Value-at-Risk to quantify precision based on rare, adverse measurement sessions. The findings demonstrate that optimizing for average performance can be catastrophically misleading, necessitating designs robust against the worst-case noise tails.
main_problem: Standard quantum metrology bounds based on averaged Fisher information fail when environmental noise is 'quenched' (frozen during a measurement session but varies between repetitions). The goal is to develop a robust certificate for achievable precision.
main_result: The true certified resource is determined by the Conditional Value-at-Risk ($	ext{CVaR}_\alpha$) of the inverse loss, which can be drastically lower than the average QFI. This leads to 'Fisher Glasses' where average metrics are misleadingly high.
method: The analysis employs advanced statistical tools like $	ext{CVaR}$ and extreme value theory applied to Fisher information derived from nuisance-projected quantum channels. It contrasts averaged channel assumptions with session-resolved, non-self-averaging statistics.
model_or_system: The study models quantum sensors (e.g., NV centers, qubits) operating in quenched environments characterized by latent disorder ($\xi$). The core mathematical framework involves projecting the full Fisher geometry onto components transverse to the nuisance directions.
key_observables: Tail-Certified Information ($	ext{ITC}_\alpha$), Averaged Quantum Fisher Information ($	ext{I}_{	ext{ann}}$), Inverse Loss Exponent ($ eta$), and Transverse Signal Action ($g^\perp$).
important_parameters: The tail exponent $ eta$ (critical for determining if certification is finite, requiring $ eta > 1$) and the confidence level $\alpha$ used in CVaR calculation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that nuisance parameters can be projected out using techniques like Schur-complement algebra, allowing the focus on the signal component transverse to the disorder plane.
figures_summary: Figures compare average QFI optimization against tail-certified designs (e.g., safe window/portfolio), showing significant recovery of certified information in the latter case. They also illustrate the dependence of the loss exponent ($ eta$) on the design architecture.
paper_structure: The paper systematically contrasts averaged vs. quenched metrology, develops the $	ext{CVaR}_\alpha$ certificate based on inverse-loss tails, establishes theoretical theorems regarding non-self-averaging, and applies these concepts to physical platforms like NV centers using specific design protocols (portfolios, reserves).
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework for quantifying the true performance limits of quantum sensors in realistic, noisy environments where noise correlations are not averaged out. It moves metrology from an idealized average bound to a robust operational guarantee.
